newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal sees further budget deficit cuts.
newsitem.headline: Portugal sees further budget deficit cuts.

text.p: Portugal's budget deficit should fall to under two percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2000 according to a three-year plan being drawn up for presentation to Lisbon's European Union partners, deputy finance minister Fernando Teixeira dos Santos said.
Teixeira dos Santos told Reuters late on Monday that the plan, which would be discussed by the cabinet this month, called for further cuts in primary spending in the three year period.
There would be no tax rises, he emphasised.

Portugal plans a budget deficit of 2.9 percent this year to meet entry criteria for the single currency, down from four percent in 1996, and the three-year plan would serve to back Lisbon's contention that its deficit-cutting was sustainable.
Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco said recently that the government hoped for a budget deficit of two percent in 1999.
"I believe we can go below that in 2000," said Teixeira dos Santos in an interview on Monday night.

He noted that a government crackdown on fiscal evasion and moves to make tax gathering more efficient had proved effective, enabling the country to boost tax revenues while not increasing income tax rates or indirect taxes.
The government intended to introduce further measures to make Portugal's tax system fairer, he said.
"The idea is not to increase the tax burden but to redistribute it more fairly," he said.
Teixeira dos Santos said that the main thrust of budgetary policy -- cutting spending while not raising taxes -- would also mark the 1998-2000 programme.
"Primary public spending, that means excluding interest payments, (will) fall through the period 1998-2000," he said.
He added however that there were limits to what Portugal could do because its education and health systems, for example, still lagged those of its more advanced European Union partners.
Nevertheless, Portugal had the advantage that reform to its social security and pension systems, while needed, was not as urgent as in some other European Union states.

"Portugal has not got the problems that some others present," he said. "Social Security is not in the short-term a source of problems for the state budget. Reform looks to the longer period," he said.
He noted that proposals on reforming the pension system based on a government white paper were due to be presented by September. Some reforms would be included in the 1998 budget, he said.
